facts.fact_text: The applicants decided to organise a demonstration in front of the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest where the reception was to be held.
The applicants did not inform the police of their intention to organise a demonstration in front of the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest.
In the afternoon of 1 December 2002, approximately 150 people assembled in front of the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest.
The applicants were among the approximately 150 people who assembled in front of the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest on 1 December 2002.
There was a loud noise during the assembly in front of the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest on 1 December 2002.
The applicants asserted before the Pest Central District Court that the demonstration on 1 December 2002 had been totally peaceful.
The police were present at the assembly in front of the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest on 1 December 2002.
The police decided to disband the assembly in front of the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest, considering that it constituted a risk to the security of the reception.
The police forced the demonstrators back to a park next to the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest.
After being forced to the park next to the Hotel Kempinski, the demonstrators dispersed after a while.
Section 6 of Law no. III of 1989 on the right of assembly (the Assembly Act) requires the police to be informed of an assembly at least three days before the date of the event.
Section 14(1) of Law no. III of 1989 on the right of assembly (the Assembly Act) requires the police to disband any assemblies held without prior notification.

The applicants pointed out that it had obviously been impossible to inform the police about the assembly three days in advance, as required by Law no. III of 1989 on the right of assembly (the Assembly Act), because the Hungarian Prime Minister had only announced his intention to attend the reception the day before the event.

The Pest Central District Court noted that the three-day time-limit for informing the police of a planned assembly could not possibly be observed if the demonstration had its roots in an event that had occurred less than three days beforehand.
The Pest Central District Court was of the view that the possible shortcomings of Law no. III of 1989 on the right of assembly (the Assembly Act) could not be remedied by the courts.
The Pest Central District Court held that the duty to inform the police about assemblies applied to every type of demonstration, including spontaneous ones.

The Pest Central District Court stated that under the relevant provisions of Hungarian domestic law in force, the fact that an assembly is peaceful is not by itself enough to dispense with the duty to inform the police.

The Pest Central District Court stated that the police had dissolved the assembly on 1 December 2002 lawfully, pursuant to section 14(1) of Law no. III of 1989 on the right of assembly (the Assembly Act).
The police decided to disband the assembly in front of the Hotel Kempinski in Budapest, considering that it constituted a risk to the security of the reception.

The Pest Central District Court found that the duty to inform the police in advance about assemblies held in public served to protect the public interest and the rights of others, namely the free flow of traffic and the right to freedom of movement.

The applicants pointed out that it had obviously been impossible to inform the police about the assembly three days in advance, as required by Law no. III of 1989 on the right of assembly (the Assembly Act), because the Hungarian Prime Minister had only announced his intention to attend the reception the day before the event.
The Pest Central District Court noted that the demonstration on 1 December 2002 had been disbanded after a minor detonation was heard.

The Pest Central District Court noted that the three-day time-limit for informing the police of a planned assembly could not possibly be observed if the demonstration had its roots in an event that had occurred less than three days beforehand.
The Pest Central District Court observed that the organisers of the demonstration on 1 December 2002 had not even attempted to notify the police.
The Budapest Regional Court found that the restrictions imposed on the applicants were necessary and proportionate.
